title: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
summary: How CLIP trains an image and a text encoder into one space with a symmetric contrastive loss, why temperature matters, how prompts become zero-shot classifiers, SigLIP's sigmoid loss, and where image search fails.
outcomes: Explain why a contrastive objective on image-caption pairs learns faster than predicting the caption text
Compute row and column softmaxes and the symmetric CLIP loss for a small batch at a given temperature
Build a zero-shot classifier from prompt templates and explain why ensembling helps
Compute the SigLIP sigmoid loss for a batch and explain why it removes the all-gather
Diagnose CLIP search failures: counting, word order, typographic attacks and the modality gap

lessons.title: Why CLIP learns from captions instead of fixed labels

blocks.md:
A standard image classifier is trained on a fixed label set. ImageNet has 1000 classes and about 1.28 million hand-labeled training images. If you later need a class the dataset never had, say *forklift* or *a whiteboard sketch*, you collect and label new data and train again.

The web already pairs billions of images with free text: alt text, titles, captions. That text names far more concepts than any label set. CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training, Radford et al., OpenAI, 2021) asks: can a model learn visual concepts from this natural language supervision, then recognize new categories just from their names?

The CLIP team built a dataset of **400 million (image, text) pairs** from the internet, which the paper calls WIT (WebImageText). To cover many concepts they searched with a large list of queries built from Wikipedia words and bigrams, Wikipedia article titles and WordNet synsets, and kept up to 20,000 pairs per query to balance the result.

The obvious way to use these pairs is to train an image model to *generate* the caption word by word, like an image captioner. The paper tried that first.

blocks.prompt: The paper compared three objectives by how fast each learns ImageNet zero-shot: (a) a transformer predicting the exact caption, (b) a model predicting the caption's bag of words, (c) a contrastive model that only picks which caption in the batch fits the image. Rank them slowest to fastest.
blocks.reveal:
Slowest to fastest: **exact caption, then bag of words, then contrastive.** In the paper's Figure 2, a 63M-parameter caption transformer learned ImageNet recognition 3x slower than the bag-of-words predictor, and swapping the predictive objective for a contrastive one gave a further 4x efficiency gain.

The reason: predicting the exact words is hard because the same photo can be described in endless ways. Picking which text *as a whole* goes with which image is an easier proxy task that still forces the model to learn what the image shows.

blocks.md:
So CLIP uses two separate encoders, one per modality (a *modality* is a kind of input: images or text):

- An **image encoder**: a ResNet or a Vision Transformer (ViT), which cuts the image into patches and runs a transformer over them.
- A **text encoder**: a transformer like GPT-2's. The base model is 12 layers, 512 wide, 8 heads, 63M parameters, with a 49,152-token byte-pair vocabulary and at most 76 tokens. The activation at the final [EOS] token is the text's feature vector.

Each encoder's output goes through one **linear projection** into a shared embedding space, then is **L2-normalized** to unit length, so a dot product between an image vector and a text vector is their cosine similarity.

blocks.title: CLIP's two towers meet in one embedding space

scenes.caption: A batch of N images goes through the image encoder. A single linear layer maps each feature vector into the shared space, and normalization puts it on the unit sphere.
The N captions from the same batch go through the text transformer in parallel. The paper uses only a linear projection here too, not the nonlinear head common in self-supervised vision.
Every image vector is dotted with every text vector, giving an N x N matrix of cosine similarities. Only the N diagonal pairs actually came together on the web.
The loss rewards high similarity for the N true pairs and low similarity for the N squared minus N wrong pairings. Gradients flow back into both encoders, so they learn one shared space.

blocks.md: Training details from the paper: both encoders start from scratch (no ImageNet weights, no pretrained language model), the only data augmentation is a random square crop, every model trains for 32 epochs with Adam, and the batch is **32,768 pairs**. The largest models were a ResNet scaled up to about 64x the compute of ResNet-50 (RN50x64) and a ViT-L/14.

CLIP does not learn to describe images. It learns two encoders whose outputs agree: a matching image and caption land close together in one shared vector space, and non-matching ones land apart. Everything else in this course (zero-shot classification, retrieval, the failure modes) follows from that geometry.

blocks.question: Why does CLIP project both encoders into one shared space and L2-normalize the result?
options: So images can be decoded back into captions
So a single dot product directly measures image-text similarity on a fixed scale
So the text encoder can reuse the image encoder's weights
Because normalization is what makes the encoders train from scratch
blocks.explain: With both vectors in the same space and of unit length, their dot product is their cosine similarity, a number between -1 and 1 that is comparable across every pair. CLIP has no decoder, the two towers share no weights, and training from scratch is a separate choice.

lessons.title: The contrastive loss on a 4 x 4 batch

blocks.md:
Recall from the embeddings course that a softmax turns scores into probabilities, and cross-entropy is the negative log of the probability given to the right answer. CLIP applies both to a similarity matrix.

Take a toy batch of N = 4 pairs: photos of a dog, a cat, a red car and a bird, with captions *a dog running on grass*, *a cat asleep on a sofa*, *a red car parked outside*, *a small bird on a branch*. Suppose the encoders currently give the cosine similarities below (made-up toy numbers; rows are images, columns are captions).

scenes.caption: Raw cosine similarities s_ij. Each true pair sits on the diagonal. Note the cat photo scores 0.26 with the dog caption, close to its own 0.29: a hard negative.
The training signal: for each row, the diagonal cell is the right answer among 4 choices. The same holds for each column.
Divide by the temperature tau = 0.07 (CLIP's starting value), which multiplies every cosine by 14.29. These are the logits.
Softmax over each row: for each image, a probability over the 4 captions. The cat row gives only 0.55 to its caption and 0.36 to the dog caption.
Softmax over each column instead: for each caption, a probability over the 4 images. The dog caption gives 0.63 to the dog photo and 0.31 to the cat photo.
The loss reads only the diagonal of each softmax. The lowest diagonal probabilities (cat row 0.55, cat column 0.61, dog column 0.63) produce most of the loss and the largest gradients.

blocks.caption: Image-to-text loss (softmax over each row) and text-to-image loss (softmax over each column), averaged. Here s_ij is the cosine of image i and caption j and tau is the temperature.

blocks.md:
Work it through for the batch at $\tau = 0.07$. Row losses are $-\ln$ of the diagonal row probabilities: 0.409 (dog), 0.594 (cat), 0.082 (car), 0.259 (bird), mean $\mathcal{L}_{\text{img}} = 0.336$. Column losses: 0.466, 0.491, 0.102, 0.277, mean $\mathcal{L}_{\text{txt}} = 0.334$. The total is their average, **0.335**.

The two directions are not identical. The cat row is hurt by one confusable caption, while the dog and cat columns are each hurt by one confusable image, the other pet photo. Using both directions trains the image tower to separate captions and the text tower to separate images.

The paper calls this a symmetric cross-entropy over the similarity scores and traces it to the multi-class N-pair loss (Sohn, 2016), popularized as the **InfoNCE** loss by Oord et al. (2018). The other N squared minus N pairs in the batch act as free *negatives*: no one labels them, they are simply the captions that came with other images.

blocks.code:
# Figure 3 of the CLIP paper, lightly trimmed (numpy-like pseudocode)
I_f = image_encoder(I)   # [n, d_i]
T_f = text_encoder(T)    # [n, d_t]

I_e = l2_normalize(np.dot(I_f, W_i), axis=1)   # [n, d_e]
T_e = l2_normalize(np.dot(T_f, W_t), axis=1)   # [n, d_e]

# scaled pairwise cosine similarities [n, n]
logits = np.dot(I_e, T_e.T) * np.exp(t)

labels = np.arange(n)
loss_i = cross_entropy_loss(logits, labels, axis=0)
loss_t = cross_entropy_loss(logits, labels, axis=1)
loss = (loss_i + loss_t) / 2
blocks.caption: t is a learned scalar; exp(t) is 1/tau. The labels are just 0..n-1 because pair i sits on the diagonal.

blocks.md: A common misreading: the off-diagonal pairs are not known to be unrelated. Two captions in a batch may both describe dogs. The loss still pushes them apart, so duplicates and near-duplicates in a batch become false negatives. With 32,768 pairs per batch this is noise the model tolerates, not something the loss detects.

blocks.question: In the toy batch, which single change would lower the image-to-text loss the most?
options: Raise the car photo's similarity to its caption from 0.33 to 0.40
Lower the bird photo's similarity to the car caption from 0.10 to 0.05
Lower the cat photo's similarity to the dog caption from 0.26 to 0.15
Raise every similarity in the matrix by 0.05
blocks.explain: The cat row has the highest row loss (0.594) because the dog caption competes at 0.26 vs 0.29. Removing that hard negative helps most. The car row is already at 0.92 probability, the bird-car cell is tiny after the exponential, and adding the same constant to a whole row leaves its softmax unchanged.

blocks.question: A teammate computes only the row-wise softmax loss (image to text) and drops the column-wise term. What does training lose?
options: The column term: no softmax ever asks each caption to pick its own image out of the batch, so text-to-image retrieval gets no direct signal
Nothing, because the column softmax is the transpose of the row softmax
The temperature, because it only appears in the column term
The negatives, because rows contain only the positive pair
blocks.explain: Row and column softmaxes normalize over different sets (captions per image vs images per caption), so their values differ, as the toy shows (0.66 vs 0.63 for the dog pair). The temperature scales both terms, and each row has N minus 1 negatives.

lessons.title: Temperature: why CLIP multiplies cosines by up to 100

blocks.md:
Cosine similarities live in $[-1, 1]$, and in practice the gaps between them are small, a few hundredths in our toy. Fed straight into a softmax, such small gaps produce almost uniform probabilities. The **temperature** $\tau$ fixes this: the logits are $s_{ij}/\tau$, so a small $\tau$ stretches small cosine gaps into large logit gaps.

CLIP does not hand-tune $\tau$. The paper learns it directly as a log-parameterized scalar (the pseudocode multiplies by $e^t$), initialized to the equivalent of $\tau = 0.07$ (a logit scale of about 14.3) and clipped so the logits are never scaled by more than 100, which the authors found necessary for training stability.

blocks.prompt: Same 4 x 4 batch, but with no temperature ($\tau = 1$, logits equal the raw cosines). What will the total loss be, roughly?
blocks.reveal:
About **1.26**, barely below $\ln 4 = 1.386$, the loss of a model that guesses uniformly among 4 captions. Every row softmax lands between 0.22 and 0.30, because $e^{0.31}$ and $e^{0.24}$ are nearly equal.

The embeddings already rank every true pair first in its row, yet the loss says the model knows almost nothing. Without a temperature the gradient keeps pushing even on pairs that are ranked correctly, and it cannot focus on the hard negatives.

blocks.title: Row softmax of the same batch at three temperatures

scenes.caption: tau = 1: probabilities are nearly uniform. Total symmetric loss 1.26, close to ln 4 = 1.386.
tau = 0.07 (CLIP's initial value, logit scale 14.29): the diagonal stands out, the cat row still splits 0.55 vs 0.36. Total loss 0.335.
tau = 0.01 (logit scale 100, the cap): a 0.03 cosine gap becomes a 3-logit gap, so even the cat row gives 0.95 to its caption. Total loss 0.008.

blocks.md:
Why not just fix $\tau$ very small from the start? A smaller $\tau$ makes the loss focus harder on the few most confusable pairs and makes the softmax saturate, so already-correct pairs stop contributing. Learning $\tau$ lets the model sharpen the distribution as its embeddings get better.

The modality gap paper (Liang et al., 2022) reports that CLIP's final learned temperature is $\tau = 1/100$, the clip value. That is why CLIP code multiplies cosines by 100 before a softmax at inference time, as in the OpenCLIP README example.

blocks.title: Dog-row loss as the logit scale grows

params.name: m
params.label: cosine margin over the hard negative

scenes.caption: The dog row: the true caption beats the cat caption by m = 0.07 and the others by 0.21 and 0.17. Loss falls from 1.28 at scale 1 to 0.41 at scale 14.3 and near 0 at 100.
Shrink the margin to 0.01 (a much harder negative). The loss stays high far longer: the larger the scale, the more a small margin is rewarded or punished.
Make the margin negative (-0.03): the wrong caption now scores higher, as with a mislabeled web pair. Loss grows roughly linearly with the scale, so a large scale amplifies noisy pairs.

blocks.md: The temperature turns a ranking of small cosine gaps into a confident probability. Its value decides how sharply the loss concentrates on hard negatives, which is why CLIP learns it and caps the logit scale at 100 for stability.

blocks.question: You fine-tune CLIP on your own data and freeze the logit scale at 1 (tau = 1) by mistake. What will you most likely observe?
options: Training diverges because the logits are too large
The loss converges to zero quickly
Zero-shot accuracy is unchanged because ranking ignores the scale
The loss stays near ln N and learns slowly, since tiny cosine gaps give almost uniform softmaxes
blocks.explain: With cosines in [-1, 1] and no scaling, the softmax over N items stays close to uniform, so the loss sits near ln N, as the toy showed (1.26 vs ln 4 = 1.386). Ranking at inference does ignore the scale, but training dynamics do not.

blocks.question: Why does a larger logit scale make the loss more sensitive to mislabeled pairs?
options: Because the scale changes which caption has the highest cosine
Because when the wrong caption wins by a margin m, the row loss grows about linearly in scale times m
Because scaling by 100 overflows float16
Because the scale is applied only to the off-diagonal entries
blocks.explain: Multiplying all logits by s does not change the ranking, but for a row where a wrong caption beats the right one by m, the loss behaves like s times m for large s (see the plot with m = -0.03). The scale multiplies every entry, and overflow is avoided by subtracting the max.

lessons.title: Zero-shot classification with prompts, probes and robustness

blocks.md:
Because images and text share one space, a set of class names *becomes* a classifier. To classify an image among classes dog, cat and car:

1. Write each class into a prompt, such as *a photo of a dog.*
2. Encode each prompt with the text encoder and normalize it. These vectors are the classifier's weights.
3. Encode and normalize the image, take its cosine with each class vector, multiply by the logit scale and apply a softmax.

No labeled examples of the task are used, hence *zero-shot*. The text vectors can be computed once and cached, so classification costs one image encoding plus a small matrix multiply.

blocks.caption: f is the image encoder, g the text encoder, s the logit scale (100 for trained CLIP).

blocks.md:
Toy example. A dog photo has these cosines with three prompts built from the template *a photo of a {label}.*: dog 0.30, cat 0.26, car 0.12. At scale 100 the logits are 30, 26 and 12, so the softmax gives **dog 0.982, cat 0.018, car 0.000**. At scale 1 the same cosines would give 0.358, 0.344 and 0.299: the ranking is identical, but the scale decides how confident the output looks.

Now a second template, *a sketch of a {label}.*, gives dog 0.24, cat 0.26, car 0.15, and the softmax picks **cat** (0.881). One template can be unlucky.

CLIP's fix is **prompt ensembling**: average the normalized text embeddings of several templates per class, normalize again, and use that as the class vector (the OpenAI prompt-engineering notebook does exactly this). Suppose the two template embeddings of each class have cosine 0.9 with each other. The average of two unit vectors then has length $\sqrt{(2+2\cdot 0.9)}/2$, and the image's cosine with the renormalized class vector is $(c_A + c_B)/\sqrt{3.8}$: dog 0.277, cat 0.267, car 0.139. At scale 100 that is **dog 0.736, cat 0.264**, back to the right answer.

blocks.title: Zero-shot probabilities for one dog photo

scenes.caption: Template A (a photo of a {label}.) at logit scale 1: nearly uniform, 0.358 / 0.344 / 0.299, though dog already ranks first.
Same template at the trained scale 100: dog 0.982. The scale changes confidence, not the ranking.
Template B (a sketch of a {label}.) at scale 100 prefers cat, 0.881. A single prompt can mislead the classifier.
Ensemble of A and B, averaged in embedding space and renormalized: dog 0.736, cat 0.264. Averaging smooths out one template's quirks.

blocks.md:
What the paper measured:

- The template *A photo of a {label}.* alone improves ImageNet zero-shot accuracy by 1.3% over bare class names, since web captions are rarely a single word.
- Ensembling 80 templates adds another 3.5%, almost 5% together. Averaged over 36 datasets, prompt engineering and ensembling gain almost 5 points, similar to using 4x more compute.
- Bare names suffer from **polysemy**: ImageNet has both construction cranes and the bird, and *boxer* in Oxford Pets is a dog breed, not an athlete.

The best CLIP model reaches **76.2%** zero-shot top-1 on ImageNet, matching the original fully supervised ResNet-50 without using any of its 1.28 million labeled training images.

Zero-shot is not the only way to use the image encoder. A **linear probe** freezes the encoder and fits a logistic-regression classifier on its embeddings using labeled data. On the paper's 27-dataset suite, zero-shot CLIP beat a fully supervised linear probe on ResNet-50 features on 16 datasets, while CLIP's best linear probe beat the strongest ImageNet model then available (Noisy Student EfficientNet-L2) on 21 of 27.

Zero-shot is weak where web captions rarely go: on satellite images, tumor detection, synthetic object counting (CLEVRCounts) and traffic signs it trails the ResNet-50 probe by a wide margin.

scenes.caption: A supervised ResNet-101 trained on ImageNet: 76.2% on ImageNet, but it falls apart on renditions (37.7%), ObjectNet (32.6%), sketches (25.2%) and adversarially filtered photos (2.7%).
Zero-shot CLIP with the same 76.2% on ImageNet keeps far more accuracy on every shifted set, for example 88.9% on ImageNet-R and 77.1% on ImageNet-A, closing up to 75% of the robustness gap.

blocks.md: Robustness does not survive adapting CLIP to ImageNet. Fitting a logistic-regression classifier on CLIP features with ImageNet labels raised ImageNet accuracy by 9.2% to 85.4%, yet average accuracy across the shifted datasets slightly decreased. Gains on the training distribution and robustness are different things.

blocks.question: You build a zero-shot classifier for 3 product categories and it often confuses two of them. Which change follows CLIP's recipe and costs nothing per prediction?
options: Average the normalized embeddings of several prompt templates per class, renormalize, and cache them
Run the image encoder once per prompt and average the image embeddings
Lower the logit scale from 100 to 1 so the softmax is less confident
Replace the softmax with an argmax over raw cosines
blocks.explain: Ensembling in embedding space gives one cached vector per class, so inference cost equals a single prompt, and the paper reports it reliably helps. The image is encoded once regardless of prompts. Changing the scale or using argmax leaves the ranking, and so the confusions, unchanged.

blocks.question: Zero-shot CLIP and an ImageNet-trained ResNet-101 both score 76.2% on ImageNet. On ImageNet Sketch, which outcome matches the paper?
options: Both drop to about 25%, since accuracy on ImageNet predicts accuracy under shift
ResNet-101 does better because it saw ImageNet labels
CLIP keeps 60.2% while ResNet-101 falls to 25.2%
CLIP drops to near chance because sketches are rare on the web
blocks.explain: Figure 13 shows zero-shot CLIP at 60.2% on ImageNet Sketch vs 25.2% for ResNet-101 despite equal ImageNet accuracy. Models trained on one dataset's labels learn shortcuts specific to it; CLIP's zero-shot classifier never fits ImageNet's distribution.

lessons.title: SigLIP's sigmoid loss and how CLIP training scales

blocks.md:
The softmax loss couples every pair in the batch: to normalize one row you need the similarity of that image with *every* caption. In data-parallel training on many devices, each device must all-gather the embeddings from all the others before it can normalize, and the SigLIP paper notes this usually materializes a memory-heavy $|B| \times |B|$ similarity matrix (CLIP itself sharded it so each GPU computed only the similarities its local pairs need). The softmax is also computed twice, once per direction.

**SigLIP** (Zhai et al., 2023) replaces it with a **sigmoid loss** that treats every (image, text) cell as an independent yes-or-no question: is this a matching pair? Diagonal cells have label $z_{ij} = +1$, all others $-1$.

blocks.tex: \mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{i=1}^{|B|}\sum_{j=1}^{|B|}\log\sigma\big(z_{ij}\,(t\,x_i\cdot y_j + b)\big),\qquad z_{ij}=\begin{cases}1 & i=j\\ -1 & i\neq j\end{cases}
blocks.caption: x_i and y_j are normalized image and text embeddings, t = exp(t') a learned temperature, b a learned bias, sigma the logistic sigmoid.

blocks.md:
The bias $b$ matters because a batch of $|B|$ pairs has $|B|$ positives and $|B|^2 - |B|$ negatives. Without it, the paper notes, the many negatives dominate early training and cause large initial steps to correct that imbalance. SigLIP initializes $t' = \ln 10$ (so $t = 10$) and $b = -10$, which starts the model close to the prior that almost every pair is a non-match.

Apply that to our toy batch: the logits are $10 s_{ij} - 10$, between $-9.3$ and $-6.7$. Every pair gets match probability of at most about 0.001 (from 0.0001 to 0.0012).

blocks.title: SigLIP match probabilities on the same batch

scenes.caption: At initialization (t = 10, b = -10) every cell has sigmoid probability of at most about 0.001 of being a match. Negatives are already right; only the 4 positives are wrong.
Illustrative later values t = 50, b = -12 (chosen by hand, not from the paper): positives rise to 0.97, 0.92, 0.99 and 0.88.
But two negatives are now judged matches: the dog caption for the cat photo (0.73) and the cat caption for the dog photo (0.50). Each cell is graded alone, with no row or column normalization.

blocks.title: Per-pair sigmoid loss, -log sigma(z times logit)

scenes.caption: At initialization the loss sits entirely on the diagonal: about 7 nats per positive, almost 0 per negative. Total loss divided by |B| = 4 is 6.98.
At t = 50, b = -12 the positives cost little (0.03 to 0.13). The two dog/cat confusions now carry most of the loss, 1.31 and 0.69. Total over 4 is 0.57, of which 0.51 comes from negatives.

blocks.md:
Because each cell's loss needs only its own logit, the sum can be computed block by block. SigLIP's chunked implementation keeps each device's images in place and passes text embeddings around the devices in a ring: each device scores its local images against the visiting texts, adds to its loss, and passes the texts on. There is no all-gather, and only one small per-device block is in memory at any time.

Findings from the paper:

- In the locked-image (SigLiT) batch-size sweep, the sigmoid loss is significantly better than softmax when the batch is **smaller than 16k**; as the batch grows, the gap closes.
- They trained at batch sizes up to **one million**, but gains saturate: around **32k** is sufficient.
- With Locked-image Tuning (a frozen pretrained image encoder, only the text tower trains), a SigLiT model reached 84.5% ImageNet zero-shot on four TPUv4 chips in two days.

blocks.prompt: SigLIP with a batch of 32k computes about a billion independent binary losses per step. Softmax CLIP with the same batch computes 2 x 32k cross-entropy terms. Which one needs the full similarity matrix in one place?
blocks.reveal:
**Only softmax CLIP.** Each softmax term needs the sum of exponentials over a whole row or column, so the full set of similarities for that row must be gathered before the term can be finished (in practice an all-gather of embeddings and a $|B| \times |B|$ matrix).

SigLIP's binary terms are independent, so devices can each compute a block, swap text chunks and add partial sums, never materializing the whole matrix. More terms, but simpler and more memory-friendly ones.

blocks.md:
**Open reproductions and scaling.** OpenAI released CLIP weights but not WIT. **OpenCLIP** is an open-source reimplementation, and Cherti et al. (2022) used it with the public **LAION** datasets (LAION-5B has about 5 billion image-text pairs) to train models on up to 2 billion pairs. They found **power-law** improvements in zero-shot classification, retrieval, linear probing and fine-tuning as model size, data and samples seen grow.

Their ViT-L/14 on LAION-2B scored 75.2% zero-shot on ImageNet vs 75.5% for OpenAI's on WIT-400M, but 71.1 vs 61.1 recall@5 (the share of text queries whose matching image is in the top 5 results) on MS-COCO image retrieval. OpenAI's models scaled better on classification and OpenCLIP's on retrieval; the authors attribute this to the training data, since architecture and recipe were matched and batch-size changes did not explain it.

When choosing a pretrained image-text model, look at results on your task type. The scaling paper shows the same architecture trained on different web data can rank differently on classification and on retrieval.

blocks.question: Your team trains an image-text model on 8 GPUs and can only fit a batch of 4,096 pairs. Based on the SigLIP paper, which loss should you prefer and why?
options: Softmax, because sigmoid needs batches over one million to work
Sigmoid, because it beat softmax clearly at batch sizes below 16k
Softmax, because sigmoid ignores negatives
Either, since both losses are identical below 32k
blocks.explain: The paper reports sigmoid significantly outperforming softmax when the batch is under 16k, with the gap closing at larger batches. Sigmoid uses all negatives, as independent binary terms, and does not need huge batches; one million was tested to show saturation.

blocks.question: In the SigLIP toy at t = 50 and b = -12, the cat photo and the dog caption have cosine 0.26, giving a logit of +1.0. What would lowering the bias b from -12 to -14 do to that cell?
options: Nothing, because the bias cancels in the sigmoid
It raises its match probability, increasing the loss
It changes only the positive cells
It lowers its logit to -1.0, so the pair is now judged a non-match and its loss falls
blocks.explain: The logit is t times cosine plus b: 50 x 0.26 - 14 = -1.0, so sigma gives 0.27 match probability and the negative's loss drops from 1.31 to about 0.31. The bias shifts every cell, which is why SigLIP learns it: it sets the threshold between match and non-match.

lessons.title: Image search with CLIP, the modality gap, and where it fails

blocks.md:
The most common production use of CLIP embeddings is **search**. Offline, encode every image in the collection once, normalize, and store the vectors in a nearest-neighbor index (FAISS is a common choice; with unit vectors, maximum inner product equals maximum cosine). Online, encode the query with the text encoder for text-to-image search, or with the image encoder for image-to-image search, normalize it, and fetch the top k neighbors.

Since the softmax scale does not change the ranking, retrieval needs no temperature at all: just cosines.

scenes.caption: Offline: every photo is embedded once and stored. Re-embedding is needed only if you switch models, because vectors from different models live in different spaces.
Online text-to-image search: one text encoding per query, then a nearest-neighbor lookup. This is zero-shot classification turned around, with the photos as the candidates.
Image-to-image search reuses the image encoder for the query. Scores from this path are image-image cosines, which sit on a different scale than text-image cosines.

blocks.md:
Why different scales? **The modality gap** (Liang et al., 2022): in CLIP's shared space, image embeddings and text embeddings occupy two separate regions. On 5,000 MS-COCO pairs, the distance between the mean image embedding and the mean text embedding is 0.82, on a unit sphere. The paper traces this to two causes:

1. A *cone effect*: a deep network, even with random weights, maps all inputs into a narrow cone, and two separately initialized encoders produce two different cones, so the gap exists at initialization.
2. The contrastive loss at CLIP's low temperature ($\tau = 1/100$) has its minimum near the existing gap and pushes back against closing it; at high temperatures the gap tends to close.

Our toy numbers echo this: true pairs scored only about 0.3, far from 1.

Do not compare scores across modalities with one threshold. Image-image cosines and text-image cosines come from different regions of the space, so a cutoff tuned for text queries will not transfer to image queries, and a mixed index of image and text vectors will tend to rank same-modality items together.

**Failure modes** to test before shipping:

- **Counting and systematic tasks.** The CLIP paper reports that CLIP struggles to count objects (CLEVRCounts) and is near random on novel tasks like classifying the distance to the nearest car in a photo. It also gets only 88% on handwritten MNIST digits, below logistic regression on raw pixels, because such images are almost absent from its training data.
- **Fine-grained classes** such as car models, flower species and aircraft variants are weak zero-shot compared with task-specific models.
- **Composition and word order.** The ARO benchmark (Yuksekgonul et al., 2023) asks models to choose between captions like *the horse is eating the grass* and *the grass is eating the horse*. CLIP scored 56% on spatial relations and 62% on attribute binding, near the 50% chance level. The authors argue contrastive training on retrieval data rewards a bag-of-words shortcut.

**Typographic attacks.** CLIP learned to read rendered text, and text in an image can override what the image shows. In OpenAI's Multimodal Neurons article (Goh et al., 2021), a zero-shot CLIP classifier labels a photo of an apple *Granny Smith* with probability 0.856. Stick a handwritten paper note saying *iPod* on the same apple and the prediction becomes *iPod* with probability 0.997.

For retrieval this means a query for a product can surface images that merely contain the product's name, such as signs, packaging or memes.

blocks.title: A typographic attack on zero-shot CLIP

scenes.caption: A photo of an apple: zero-shot CLIP says Granny Smith with probability 0.856 and iPod with 0.004 (numbers from the Distill article's figure data).
The same apple with a handwritten paper label reading iPod: iPod 0.997, Granny Smith 0.001. The written word outweighs the visual evidence.

blocks.code:
import torch, open_clip
from PIL import Image

model, _, preprocess = open_clip.create_model_and_transforms(
    'ViT-B-32', pretrained='laion2b_s34b_b79k')
model.eval()
tokenizer = open_clip.get_tokenizer('ViT-B-32')

with torch.no_grad():
    imgs = torch.stack([preprocess(Image.open(p)) for p in paths])
    img_emb = model.encode_image(imgs)
    img_emb /= img_emb.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True)   # unit vectors

    q = model.encode_text(tokenizer(['a red bicycle leaning on a wall']))
    q /= q.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True)

scores = (q @ img_emb.T).squeeze(0)      # cosine similarities
top = scores.topk(5)
print([(paths[i], round(s.item(), 3)) for s, i in zip(top.values, top.indices)])

blocks.question: A photo search built on CLIP returns, for the query 'three dogs on a beach', many images with one or two dogs. Which explanation is best supported by the sources?
options: The index is approximate, so it drops the best matches
The logit scale was not applied at query time
CLIP embeddings encode counts poorly; the paper reports it struggles with counting objects
The text encoder truncates queries longer than 3 words
blocks.explain: The CLIP paper lists counting among its systematic weaknesses (CLEVRCounts). The logit scale does not affect the ranking, the text encoder accepts up to 76 tokens, and an approximate index would not systematically return the wrong count.

blocks.question: You index both product photos and product descriptions in one CLIP vector index and query it with a photo. What does the modality gap predict?
options: Results skew toward other photos, because image embeddings sit in a separate region from text embeddings
Results are evenly mixed, because the space is shared
Results skew toward descriptions, because text embeddings are closer to every image
The query fails, because image queries need the text encoder
blocks.explain: Liang et al. show image and text embeddings form separate regions (mean distance 0.82 on MS-COCO for CLIP). An image query is therefore closer to images in general than to text, so same-modality items crowd the top results even when a description matches better.
